rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention pattern will guide a narrower gradient window and subsequent slope and temperature tests.

Injection 1 already achieves the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient while keeping its window and temperature fixed to test whether full resolution can be maintained with faster elution.
The 6-minute gradient retains full resolution with a minimum R of 2.46. Test the next shorter gradient to reduce elution time while approaching the resolution limit of the earliest pair.

Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The earliest pair may fall below R = 1.5; if so, the fully resolved 4-minute method remains the benchmark for temperature refinement.
Keep the fast gradient fixed and test whether higher temperature improves selectivity for the unresolved earliest pair. The fully resolved 4-minute method is retained as a maximum-CRF fallback.

Heating reduced resolution, so test the lowest temperature with the same fast gradient to measure selectivity in the opposite direction. This will show whether cooling alone can rescue the earliest pair before adjusting the gradient window.

Cooling improved the critical pair to R = 1.23; narrowing the gradient should provide the additional separation needed for full credit. The final peak will likely elute during the hold, so this run tests the tradeoff between early-pair resolution and late retention.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope that resolved every pair in injection 7. The higher final organic fraction should accelerate the last peak; this tests whether the earliest pair retains sufficient resolution.

Shift the window upward another 0.10 while retaining the successful gradient slope and temperature. This should shorten late elution further, provided the higher starting organic fraction does not compromise the earliest pair.

Raise the starting organic fraction one grid step to narrow the gradient and potentially shorten the last peak's retention while improving gradient selectivity. Monitor the earliest pair for loss of retention; injection 9 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.
Increase temperature one step while retaining injection 10's gradient to shorten late elution. The critical pair's R of 1.77 provides some margin for the selectivity loss observed on heating.

Test whether narrowing the gradient by raising phi0 can further shorten elution without losing full resolution. The first peak is already close to the unretained region, so this probes the upper starting-organic boundary while retaining injection 11 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Return phi0 to 0.30 to restore early retention, and narrow the gradient to compensate for the resolution loss expected from another 5 C increase. This tests an alternative fast, fully resolved method near the established selectivity boundary.

Shift injection 13's window downward while preserving its slope to keep the earliest pair away from the unretained region. This tests whether improved early retention restores full resolution at 35 C, while monitoring the final peak for added hold time.

Reduce phi1 one step to make the gradient shallower and lift the critical pair from R = 1.42 toward full resolution. The last peak should remain comfortably within 10 minutes, allowing maximum CRF despite some additional hold time.

Back off one temperature step from injection 13 to restore early-pair resolution while retaining a high final organic fraction for rapid late elution. This tests a potentially better-resolved alternative to injection 11 with only a small time increase.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 16 to move the first peak away from the near-unretained region while retaining rapid late elution. This tests a less boundary-sensitive maximum-CRF alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower temperature one step from injection 17 to improve its marginal early-pair resolution while keeping the first peak well retained. This should provide a larger resolution margin with only a modest increase in elution time; the maximum CRF is already secured.

Raise phi0 one step from injection 18 to test whether its resolution margin can be retained with slightly faster late elution. At this starting fraction, cooling previously kept the first peak above the near-unretained region.

Narrow injection 19's gradient one step to increase the critical pair's resolution margin, accepting a modest increase in final-peak retention. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 20 to improve early retention while testing whether its resolution margin is preserved. This explores a maximum-CRF alternative less close to the unretained region; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method, injection 11, while keeping its gradient fixed. This directly checks the speed–resolution boundary; if the earliest pair falls below 1.5, retain 30 C as the preferred temperature for this gradient.

Test the intermediate temperature between injections 21 and 14 to shorten the fully resolved 25 C run while retaining sufficient early-pair resolution. Injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Raise phi0 one step from injection 23 to test a slightly faster maximum-CRF method with a modest resolution margin. Nearby runs suggest the earliest pair should remain resolved, while injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed option.

Lower temperature one step from injection 15 to move its borderline early-pair resolution clearly above 1.5 while keeping all peaks well within 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
